newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - Analysts sceptical of pulp price hike talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Analysts sceptical of pulp price hike talk.

text.p: European pulp producers boosted paper industry shares on Monday with a flurry of hopes for pulp price hikes soon, but analysts said the talk was not yet realistic as pulp stocks remain massive.
Pulp prices -- a key indicator for the volatile paper industry's business cycle -- could rise sustainably only when the market was closer to balance, they said.
Swedish media earlier reported that U.S. producers Georgia-Pacific and Stone were planning to raise the price of northern long-fibre pulp to $580 per tonne in May from $520 now.
That sparked comments from European producers -- including Sweden's Sodra and Finland's Metsa-Botnia and Portugal's Portucel -- that they might follow.
Helped by Wall Street's rebound on Friday and a strong dollar, forest industry shares in Sweden and Finland rose three to four percent. But few analysts were impressed.
"This is cloud cuckoo land," said Dennis Christie, paper industry analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London. "You have to think about the equilibrium of the market."
Enskilda's Lars Kjellberg in Stockholm agreed, saying that higher prices were unlikely this spring and the comments were probably aimed at shifting inventories.

"That's all you achieve with this sort of announcement now, and that is not meaningful," he said. "I don't really see why come with announcements at this stage -- why not wait a while and let stocks fall, then do it?"

Pulp prices plunged in late 1995 and early last year to current depressed levels -- around $520 per tonne for northern softwood pulp -- as weak underlying demand for paper invited users to build up stocks.
At 2.1 million tonnes in February, monthly North American and Scandinavian (Norscan) pulp producer stocks were up 70,000 tonnes over January -- their ninth consecutive increase.

Although analysts expect a fall in March due to strengthening global economic growth, they said this was unlikely to take stocks close enough to the 1.5 million tonnes level generally associated with a pulp price recovery.

Few were willing to forecast specific levels for March stocks, expected some time next week, but most expected a relatively brisk decline. "Anything less than 100,000 would be a disappointment," Kjellberg said.

If stocks fall clearly faster than expected, the industry's hopes for higher prices may become more realistic, particularly if producers make substantial output cuts to bolster prices. Some analysts were already optimistic.
Current pulp prices were already unprofitable to many producers, they said, so downtime would do little damage.

"Hopes to reach $580 (per tonne) are probably too high ... but I do expect rises -- $560 would already be quite good, and the price could approach $600 after the holiday season," said Aktia Bank analyst Paivi Palomaki.
